distr::Logistic¶

The logistic distribution: a bell-shaped curve slightly heavier-tailed than the normal, whose distribution function is the logistic (sigmoid) function.

Signature¶

pluss::Series distr::pdf(dst::Logistic, const pluss::Series& x, const std::vector<double>& params);
pluss::Series distr::logpdf(dst::Logistic, const pluss::Series& x, const std::vector<double>& params);
pluss::Series distr::cdf(dst::Logistic, const pluss::Series& x, const std::vector<double>& params);
pluss::Series distr::logcdf(dst::Logistic, const pluss::Series& x, const std::vector<double>& params);
pluss::Series distr::sample(dst::Logistic, const std::vector<double>& params, std::initializer_list<std::int64_t> sizes, pluss::Config cfg = {}, std::uint64_t seed = 0);

What It Does¶

The logistic distribution has a distribution function that is the logistic function 1/(1 + exp(-(x - location)/scale)), which makes it the natural error model of logistic regression and growth curves. Its density is symmetric and bell-shaped, close to a normal with standard deviation 1.8 × scale, with exponentially decaying but heavier tails. Its variance is pi² scale² / 3.

The parameters, in the order of the params list:

Parameter

Constraint

Meaning

location

any real

the centre: the mean, median and mode

scale

> 0

the scale of the logistic function; the standard deviation is pi scale / sqrt(3)

Support: all real numbers.

The object form of this family, with the same functions as methods, is on its own page: distr::Logistic.

Parameters¶

const pluss::Series& x

The points at which to evaluate, a Series of any shape; the result has the same shape. Points outside the support have density zero and distribution value 0 or 1.

const std::vector<double>& params

The parameters of the family, in the order shown in the table above. A list of the wrong length is refused.

std::initializer_list<std::int64_t> sizes

The shape of the array of random draws, for example {n} or {rows, columns}.

pluss::Config cfg

The dtype and platform of the draws; the default is Float32 on the CPU, so request Float64 when precision matters.

std::uint64_t seed

The seed of the stream. The same seed always gives the same draws; a seed of 0 is a fixed default, not a random one.

Returns¶

pdf, logpdf, cdf and logcdf return a Series of the shape of x; sample returns a Series of the requested shape.

Errors¶

  • Parameters outside their valid range are refused with an error that names the requirement (scale must be positive).

  • A params list of the wrong length is refused.

Practical Examples¶

Example 1¶

Example 1 evaluates the density (mass) function, the distribution function and the log-density of the Logistic on a small grid with distr::pdf, distr::cdf and distr::logpdf.

#include <pluss/ma.h>

#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

namespace distr = pluss::subsp::stats::distr;
namespace dst = distr::dst;

int main() {
  const auto f64 = pluss::Config{}.with_dtype(pluss::ScalarType::Float64);
  std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(5);

  const auto x = pluss::make_series({-6.0, -2.0, 0.0, 0.5, 2.0, 7.0}, f64);
  const std::vector<double> params = {0.5, 1.2};

  std::cout << "x:";
  for (double v : x.pull<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
  std::cout << '\n';
  std::cout << "pdf:";
  for (double v : distr::pdf(dst::Logistic, x, params).pull<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
  std::cout << '\n';
  std::cout << "cdf:";
  for (double v : distr::cdf(dst::Logistic, x, params).pull<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
  std::cout << '\n';
  std::cout << "logpdf:";
  for (double v : distr::logpdf(dst::Logistic, x, params).pull<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
  std::cout << '\n';
}

Output

x: -6.00000 -2.00000 0.00000 0.50000 2.00000 7.00000
pdf: 0.00367 0.08206 0.19955 0.20833 0.14425 0.00367
cdf: 0.00442 0.11073 0.39731 0.50000 0.77730 0.99558
logpdf: -5.60785 -2.50036 -1.61171 -1.56862 -1.93618 -5.60785

The density is largest on this grid at x = 0.5, where it is 0.20833; the distribution function runs from 0.00442 at x = -6 to 0.99558 at x = 7, and it is the running total of the density. logpdf is the logarithm of the density, for example log(0.20833) = -1.56863 at x = 0.5.

Example 2¶

Example 2 checks that the three descriptions of the same probability agree: the integral of the density (sum of the masses) over a range, the difference of the distribution function at its ends, and the fraction of random draws that land in it.

#include <pluss/ma.h>

#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

namespace distr = pluss::subsp::stats::distr;
namespace dst = distr::dst;

int main() {
  const auto f64 = pluss::Config{}.with_dtype(pluss::ScalarType::Float64);
  std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(5);
  const std::vector<double> params = {0.5, 1.2};

  // The three ways to the probability that the variable lies in [-2, 4]:
  const auto grid = pluss::series::linspace(-2.0, 4.0, 3001, f64);
  const double area = as_f64(distr::pdf(dst::Logistic, grid, params).antidiff(grid).trapezoid());

  const auto edges = pluss::make_series({-2.0, 4.0}, f64);
  const auto c = distr::cdf(dst::Logistic, edges, params).pull<double>();

  const auto draws = distr::sample(dst::Logistic, params, {200000}, f64, 7ULL);
  const double fraction = as_f64(((draws >= -2.0).to(pluss::ScalarType::Float64) * (draws <= 4.0).to(pluss::ScalarType::Float64)).mean());

  std::cout << "integral of the density: " << area << '\n';
  std::cout << "cdf(4) - cdf(-2): " << c[1] - c[0] << '\n';
  std::cout << "fraction of 200000 draws in range: " << fraction << '\n';
}

Output

integral of the density: 0.83794
cdf(4) - cdf(-2): 0.83794
fraction of 200000 draws in range: 0.83730

The integral of the density (0.83794) and the difference of the distribution function (0.83794) agree to all printed digits: they are two computations of one probability. The fraction of random draws (0.8373) differs from it by 6.40e-04, which is the size of the sampling error of a fraction of 200000 draws (a standard error of about 8.24e-04), so the density, the distribution function and the sampler describe the same distribution.

Example 3¶

Example 3 shows how the shape changes with the parameters: the density at the same points for 3 parameter settings.

#include <pluss/ma.h>

#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

namespace distr = pluss::subsp::stats::distr;
namespace dst = distr::dst;

int main() {
  const auto f64 = pluss::Config{}.with_dtype(pluss::ScalarType::Float64);
  std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(4);
  const auto x = pluss::make_series({-5.0, -2.0, 0.5, 3.0, 6.0}, f64);

  std::cout << "x:";
  for (double v : x.pull<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
  std::cout << '\n';
  std::cout << "scale 0.5:";
  for (double v : distr::pdf(dst::Logistic, x, {0.5, 0.5}).pull<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
  std::cout << '\n';
  std::cout << "scale 1  :";
  for (double v : distr::pdf(dst::Logistic, x, {0.5, 1.0}).pull<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
  std::cout << '\n';
  std::cout << "scale 2  :";
  for (double v : distr::pdf(dst::Logistic, x, {0.5, 2.0}).pull<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
  std::cout << '\n';
}

Output

x: -5.0000 -2.0000 0.5000 3.0000 6.0000
scale 0.5: 0.0000 0.0133 0.5000 0.0133 0.0000
scale 1  : 0.0041 0.0701 0.2500 0.0701 0.0041
scale 2  : 0.0282 0.0866 0.1250 0.0866 0.0282

Read down the rows: scale 0.5 peaks on this grid at x = 0.5 (value 0.5); scale 1 peaks on this grid at x = 0.5 (value 0.25); scale 2 peaks on this grid at x = 0.5 (value 0.125). The parameters move the location, the width and the shape of the curve, which is what choosing a member of the family means.

Example 4¶

Example 4 checks the distribution function against the logistic function it is named after.

#include <pluss/ma.h>

#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

namespace distr = pluss::subsp::stats::distr;
namespace dst = distr::dst;

int main() {
  const auto f64 = pluss::Config{}.with_dtype(pluss::ScalarType::Float64);
  std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(6);
  const auto x = pluss::make_series({-6.0, -2.0, 0.0, 0.5, 2.0, 7.0}, f64);
  const std::vector<double> params = {0.5, 1.2};

  const auto formula = ((-(x - 0.5) / 1.2).exp() + 1.0).reciprocal();
  const auto library = distr::cdf(dst::Logistic, x, params);

  std::cout << "x:";
  for (double v : x.pull<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
  std::cout << '\n';
  std::cout << "formula:";
  for (double v : formula.pull<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
  std::cout << '\n';
  std::cout << "distr::cdf:";
  for (double v : library.pull<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
  std::cout << '\n';
  std::cout << std::scientific << std::setprecision(2) << "largest difference: " << as_f64((formula - library).abs().max()) << '\n';
}

Output

x: -6.000000 -2.000000 0.000000 0.500000 2.000000 7.000000
formula: 0.004422 0.110727 0.397315 0.500000 0.777300 0.995578
distr::cdf: 0.004422 0.110727 0.397315 0.500000 0.777300 0.995578
largest difference: 0.00e+00

The formula and distr::cdf agree to 0 over the grid, so the library implements exactly the closed form quoted above; the same expression is the quickest way to check a parameterisation before relying on it.

Example 5¶

Example 5 confirms that the Tukey lambda distribution with lambda = 0 is the standard logistic distribution.

#include <pluss/ma.h>

#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

namespace distr = pluss::subsp::stats::distr;
namespace dst = distr::dst;

int main() {
  const auto f64 = pluss::Config{}.with_dtype(pluss::ScalarType::Float64);
  std::cout << std::scientific << std::setprecision(2);
  const auto x = pluss::make_series({-4.0, -1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 4.0}, f64);
  const std::vector<double> here = {0.0, 1.0};
  const std::vector<double> there = {0.0};

  const double dpdf = as_f64((distr::pdf(dst::Logistic, x, here) - distr::pdf(dst::TukeyLambda, x, there)).abs().max());
  const double dcdf = as_f64((distr::cdf(dst::Logistic, x, here) - distr::cdf(dst::TukeyLambda, x, there)).abs().max());
  std::cout << "largest difference in the density: " << dpdf << '\n';
  std::cout << "largest difference in the distribution function: " << dcdf << '\n';
}

Output

largest difference in the density: 0.00e+00
largest difference in the distribution function: 0.00e+00

The two largest differences are 0 for the density and 0 for the distribution function over the grid: zero up to rounding, so the two descriptions are the same distribution.
